title: Cardiovascular & Pulmonary Clinical Specialist
description: ABPTS board certification in cardiovascular and pulmonary physical therapy: case-history examination weighted toward evaluation (30%), with the outline's own frequently-, occasionally- and rarely-seen diagnoses.

units.title: Professional behaviors, leadership, education, administration and consultation
units.gate: Describe the specialist's consulting role on a cardiac or pulmonary unit with a concrete example.

objectives.text: Leadership, consultation and program administration in cardiopulmonary rehabilitation
Education of patients, families and interprofessional staff about activity, risk and self-management

units.title: Evidence-based clinical practice and critical inquiry
units.gate: Appraise a cardiopulmonary rehabilitation study and state what it justifies in practice.

objectives.text: Critical inquiry principles and methods applied to cardiopulmonary rehabilitation evidence
Clinical practice guidelines for cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation and their limits

units.title: Examination
units.gate: From a case history, select the examination that establishes exercise safety and the physiologic limit to activity.

objectives.text: History and chart review: cardiac and pulmonary diagnoses, procedures, devices, labs and medications that change the plan
Vital signs, ECG rhythm recognition and hemodynamic monitoring during examination
Pulmonary examination: breath sounds, breathing pattern, cough and airway clearance assessment
Exercise and functional testing: six-minute walk, submaximal and symptom-limited testing and when each is appropriate
Examination of the patient with lines, drains, ventilators, pacemakers, defibrillators and ventricular assist devices

units.title: Evaluation
units.gate: Interpret the full data set -- rhythm, hemodynamics, gases, imaging, labs -- for a frequently-seen diagnosis and decide whether to proceed, modify or stop.

objectives.text: Interpreting ECG, arterial blood gases, pulmonary function tests, chest imaging and laboratory values
Evaluating exercise responses in coronary disease, heart failure, dysrhythmia, hypertension and peripheral vascular disease
Evaluating the post-procedure patient: angioplasty, bypass graft, valve replacement, pacemaker and defibrillator, transplant and assist devices
Evaluating pulmonary presentations: COPD, asthma, pneumonia, atelectasis, effusion, respiratory failure, pulmonary embolism and post-operative complications
Evaluating occasionally- and rarely-seen diagnoses: cystic fibrosis, lung transplant, congenital defects, ECMO, aortic repair and pericarditis
Recognizing decompensation and emergencies that require stopping activity or escalating care

units.title: Diagnosis and prognosis
units.gate: State the physical therapy diagnosis and a realistic prognosis for a cardiopulmonary case, with the factor most likely to limit it.

objectives.text: Movement-system diagnosis in cardiovascular and pulmonary disease
Prognosis across acute, inpatient rehabilitation, outpatient and home settings

units.title: Plan of care and interventions
units.gate: Write an exercise prescription with intensity, monitoring parameters and stop criteria for a specific cardiac or pulmonary diagnosis.

objectives.text: Exercise prescription and progression in cardiac rehabilitation phases
Pulmonary rehabilitation: airway clearance, breathing retraining, inspiratory muscle training and oxygen titration
Early mobilization in the ICU, including patients on mechanical ventilation and circulatory support
Risk-factor modification and self-management education

units.title: Outcomes
units.gate: Select the outcome measure that will show change for a cardiopulmonary patient and state what change is meaningful.

objectives.text: Outcome measures for exercise capacity, dyspnea, quality of life and participation
Using outcomes to guide discharge and transition between rehabilitation phases

units.title: Diagnosis frequency distribution
units.gate: Name which category -- frequently, occasionally or rarely seen -- a given diagnosis sits in, and why that changes how much exam attention it earns.

objectives.text: Frequently-seen diagnoses (60% of items): coronary and peripheral atherosclerosis, heart failure, hypertension, dysrhythmia, myocardial infarction, pulmonary edema, COPD, pneumonia, atelectasis and respiratory failure
Occasionally-seen diagnoses (30%): aortic repair, ventricular assist devices, heart transplant, cystic fibrosis, lung resection and transplant, bronchiolitis and sarcoidosis
Rarely-seen diagnoses (10%): congenital heart defects, ECMO, lymphedema, tuberculosis, bronchopulmonary dysplasia and heart-lung transplant
